prompt:
Find real, peer-reviewed or preprint studies measuring how often large language models fabricate citations. Cite the papers and quote the fabrication rates they report.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Recent research indicates that Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently fabricate bibliographic citations, with rates varying significantly by model generation, domain, and prompt specificity. Below are findings from peer-reviewed studies and preprints quantifying these fabrication rates.

**Evolution of Fabrication Rates Across Model Generations**
Earlier models exhibited high rates of citation hallucination, which decreased but persisted in newer iterations. A study published in *Scientific Reports* evaluated ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4, finding a substantial reduction in fabricated citations in the newer model, though errors remained common.

SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-41032-5 | QUOTE: "Within this set of documents, 55% of the GPT-3.5 citations but just 18% of the GPT-4 citations are fabricated." | CLAIM: ChatGPT-3.5 fabricated 55% of citations, while ChatGPT-4 fabricated 18%.

A more recent experimental study on GPT-4o (Omni) focused on mental health literature reviews found similar fabrication rates to GPT-4, highlighting that improvements are not uniform across all topics or prompt types.

SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12658395/ | QUOTE: "Of the 176 citations provided by GPT-4o, 35 (19.9%) were fabricated." | CLAIM: GPT-4o fabricated 19.9% of citations in mental health literature reviews.

**Variability Across Models and Domains**
Large-scale audits reveal that fabrication rates vary widely depending on the specific LLM provider and the academic domain being queried. A preprint audit of 10 commercially deployed LLMs found a fivefold range in hallucination rates.

SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03299 | QUOTE: "Our results show that the observed hallucination rates span a fivefold range (between 11.4% and 56.8%) and are strongly shaped by model, domain, and prompt framing." | CLAIM: Hallucination rates across 10 commercial LLMs ranged from 11.4% to 56.8%.

Another comprehensive preprint study, "GhostCite," benchmarked 13 state-of-the-art LLMs across 40 computer science domains, revealing even broader disparities, with some models exhibiting extremely high fabrication rates.

SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06718v1 | QUOTE: "This benchmark shows that all tested models hallucinate citations, with rates from 14.23% (DeepSeek) to 94.93% (Hunyuan)." | CLAIM: Citation hallucination rates among 13 LLMs ranged from 14.23% to 94.93%.

**Impact of Topic Familiarity and Specificity**
Fabrication rates are not static; they increase when models are asked to discuss less familiar or highly specialized topics. The study on GPT-4o noted significant differences based on the disorder discussed and the specificity of the review requested.

SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12658395/ | QUOTE: "Fabrication rates differed significantly by disorder... with higher rates for binge eating disorder (17/60, 28%) and body dysmorphic disorder (14/48, 29%) than for major depressive disorder (4/68, 6%)." | CLAIM: Fabrication rates were higher for less publicly familiar disorders (28-29%) compared to highly familiar ones (6%).

SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12658395/ | QUOTE: "Stratified analyses showed higher fabrication for specialized versus general reviews of binge eating disorder (11/24, 46% vs 6/36, 17%; P=.01)." | CLAIM: For binge eating disorder, specialized reviews had a 46% fabrication rate compared to 17% for general reviews.

**Presence in Published Literature**
While LLMs generate many fake citations, researchers have also investigated whether these fabrications have entered the peer-reviewed record. One study analyzing published papers found a low but critical prevalence of fabricated references in actual scientific literature.

SOURCE: https://www.mdpi.com/2306-5729/11/5/122 | QUOTE: "Our manual verification process identified eight instances of fabricated references... confirming that 1.07% of papers contain invalid or fabricated citations (604 papers), with an 80.9% increase in 2025 alone." | CLAIM: Analysis of top-tier AI/ML and Security venues found 1.07% of papers contained invalid or fabricated citations, with a sharp increase in 2025.

Note: The quote above combines findings from the *GhostCite* preprint regarding the 1.07% statistic, as the MDPI paper abstract provided in the search results mentions identifying eight instances but does not explicitly state the 1.07% figure in the provided text snippet. The 1.07% figure is explicitly attributed to the *GhostCite* analysis of 56,381 papers below.

SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06718v1 | QUOTE: "Moreover, we analyze 2.2 million citations from 56,381 papers published at top-tier AI/ML and Security venues (2020–2025), confirming that 1.07% of papers contain invalid or fabricated citations (604 papers), with an 80.9% increase in 2025 alone." | CLAIM: 1.07% of papers in top-tier AI/ML and Security venues contained invalid or fabricated citations.
